questions.title: ERD terms
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: A thing about which data is stored, e.g. Student
A property of an entity, e.g. DateOfBirth
The degree of a relationship, e.g. one-to-many

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: What an ERD shows
questions.text: Describe what an **entity-relationship diagram** shows.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The entities (tables) of a system (1)
- the relationships between them and their type / degree (1:1, 1:M, M:M) (1)
scheme.model_answer: It shows the entities in a system and the relationships between them, including whether each is one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

questions.title: Type of relationship
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Country–Capital 1:1; Mother–Child 1:M; Student–Course M:M; Customer–Order 1:M; Actor–Film M:M

Five correct (4); four (3); three (2); one or two (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award 4 for five correct rows, 3 for four, 2 for three, 1 for one or two.

questions.title: Where the foreign key goes
questions.text: One class has many pupils; each pupil is in one class. How is this relationship created in a relational database?

options.content: PupilID is added to the Classes table as a foreign key
ClassID is added to the Pupils table as a foreign key
A link table is always needed
The two tables are combined into one

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: In a 1:M relationship the primary key of the 'one' side becomes a foreign key in the 'many' side.

questions.title: Many-to-many in a database
questions.text: A many-to-many relationship can be created directly by putting a foreign key in one of the two tables.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A many-to-many relationship needs a link (junction) table containing both foreign keys.

questions.title: Publishers and titles
questions.text:
```text
Publishers ( pub_ID, pub_name, city )
Titles     ( title_ID, title, price, pub_ID )
```

Describe the type of relationship between `Publishers` and `Titles`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Publishers (primary key pub_ID) links to the foreign key pub_ID in Titles (1)
- one-to-many: one publisher may have many titles; each title has one publisher (1)
scheme.model_answer: pub_ID, the primary key of Publishers, appears in Titles as a foreign key. The relationship is one-to-many: one publisher can publish many titles, but each title has one publisher.

questions.title: Draw the Books ERD
questions.text:
Build the entity-relationship diagram for the Books database.

```text
Publishers ( pub_ID, pub_name, city )
Titles     ( title_ID, title, price, pub_ID )
```

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities Publishers and Titles connected (1)
One-to-many relationship, many at Titles (1)
scheme.model_answer: Publishers 1 —— M Titles
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept crow's foot or labelled cardinality. M:1 drawn from Titles to Publishers is equivalent.

questions.title: Resolve many-to-many
questions.text: A student can join many clubs and a club has many students. Explain how this relationship is implemented in a relational database. Include the fields of any new table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A link / junction table is created, e.g. Memberships (1)
- containing the foreign keys StudentID and ClubID (1)
- whose composite primary key is (StudentID, ClubID); the M:M becomes two 1:M relationships (1)
scheme.model_answer: A link table Memberships(StudentID, ClubID) is created. It holds the two foreign keys, which together form a composite primary key, so Students 1—M Memberships M—1 Clubs.

questions.title: Why a link table
questions.text: Explain why a list of all the student's courses cannot simply be stored in one field of the `Students` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A field must hold a single (atomic) value (1)
- a list would break 1NF / make searching and updating difficult / need many columns; a link table stores one record per student–course pair (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each field must contain one atomic value; a list of courses in one field could not be searched or updated properly, so a link table with one record for each student–course pair is used.

questions.title: Where are the foreign keys
questions.text:
```text
Teams   ( TeamID, TeamName, City )
Players ( PlayerID, Name, Position, TeamID )
Coaches ( CoachID, Name, TeamID )
```

Each team has many players and exactly one coach. Complete the table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Teams — Players: 1:M (1), foreign key TeamID in Players
Teams — Coaches: 1:1 (1), foreign key TeamID in Coaches
Both foreign keys correct (1)

questions.title: Draw a school ERD
questions.text:
```text
Teachers ( TeacherID, Name, Subject )
Classes  ( ClassID, Room, TeacherID )
Pupils   ( PupilID, Name, ClassID )
```

Each class has one teacher, who can teach many classes. Each pupil belongs to one class. Draw the ERD.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Three entities connected correctly (1)
Teachers 1 — M Classes (1)
Classes 1 — M Pupils (1)
scheme.model_answer: Teachers 1 —— M Classes 1 —— M Pupils
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept equivalent M:1 drawn in the opposite direction.

questions.title: Steps to create an ERD
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

To draw an ERD, first identify the [[1]] (the things about which data is stored). Then decide the degree of each relationship by asking the question in [[2]] directions. Every many-to-many relationship is replaced by a [[3]] table.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) entities (2) both / two (3) link / junction

questions.title: Entities from a description
questions.text:
*A gym has many members. Each member books classes. Each class is led by one trainer, who can lead many classes. A class can be booked by many members.*

State the type of each relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Trainer — Class: one-to-many (1)
Member — Class: many-to-many (1)
Implemented with a link table, e.g. Bookings(MemberID, ClassID) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Trainer — Class: one-to-many. Member — Class: many-to-many. A Bookings link table with MemberID and ClassID.

questions.title: Draw a resolved M:M
questions.text: Students take many courses, and each course has many students. Draw an ERD that implements this relationship with a link table called `Enrolments`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Enrolments entity added between Students and Courses (with StudentID, CourseID) (1)
Students 1 — M Enrolments (1)
Courses 1 — M Enrolments (1)
scheme.model_answer: Students 1 —— M Enrolments M —— 1 Courses
scheme.ai_instructions: A direct M:M line between Students and Courses scores at most 1 mark.

questions.title: One-to-one
questions.text: Each employee is given exactly one company car, and each car is given to exactly one employee. State the type of relationship and explain how it can be created.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- One-to-one (1)
- e.g. EmployeeID as a (unique) foreign key in Cars / CarID in Employees, or combine the tables (1)
scheme.model_answer: One-to-one. CarID can be stored as a unique foreign key in the Employees table.

questions.title: Crow's foot
questions.text: In crow's foot notation, what does the "crow's foot" at the end of a relationship line show?

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: A hospital database
questions.text: A hospital stores data about **wards**, **patients** and **doctors**. Each patient is in one ward; a ward has many patients. A doctor treats many patients and a patient can be treated by many doctors.

parts.title: Relationship types
parts.text: State the type of the relationship between Ward and Patient, and between Doctor and Patient.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Ward — Patient: one-to-many (1)
Doctor — Patient: many-to-many (1)
scheme.model_answer: Ward — Patient: one-to-many. Doctor — Patient: many-to-many.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for the hospital. Resolve the many-to-many relationship with a link entity called `Treatments`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Wards 1 — M Patients (1)
Treatments entity added (1)
Patients 1 — M Treatments (1)
Doctors 1 — M Treatments (1)
scheme.model_answer: Wards 1 —— M Patients 1 —— M Treatments M —— 1 Doctors
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept a direct M:M Doctors–Patients line for the relationship marks but not the Treatments marks.

questions.title: Design for an online shop
questions.text:
An online shop stores data about **customers**, **orders** and **products**. A customer can place many orders. An order can contain many products, and a product can appear in many orders.

Describe the relationships between the entities and explain how they would be implemented in a relational database. Include the tables, primary keys and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Customer — Order is 1:M (1)
- implemented with CustomerID as a foreign key in Orders (1)
- Order — Product is M:M (1)
- resolved with a link table, e.g. OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity) (1)
- with composite primary key (OrderID, ProductID) / both foreign keys (1)
- tables listed with primary keys: Customers(CustomerID…), Orders(OrderID…), Products(ProductID…) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The relationship between customers and orders is one-to-many: Customers(CustomerID, Name, Email) is linked to Orders(OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate) by the foreign key CustomerID in Orders. Orders and products have a many-to-many relationship, which cannot be stored directly, so a link table OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity) is created. Its primary key is the composite key (OrderID, ProductID) and both fields are foreign keys to Orders and Products(ProductID, Name, Price). This gives Orders 1—M OrderLines M—1 Products.

questions.title: A library database
questions.text:
A library uses this database.

```text
Members ( MemberID, Name, Phone )
Books   ( BookID, Title, Author )
Loans   ( LoanID, MemberID, BookID, LoanDate, ReturnDate )
```

parts.title: Members and Loans
parts.text: Describe the type of relationship between the tables `Members` and `Loans`.

scheme.mark_scheme: Members (primary key MemberID) links to foreign key MemberID in Loans (1); relation is one-to-many (1)
scheme.model_answer: MemberID, the primary key of Members, is a foreign key in Loans; one member can have many loans, so it is one-to-many.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the entity-relationship diagram to show the relationships between the tables in the database.

nodes.label:
Loans
LoanID, MemberID, BookID, LoanDate, ReturnDate

scheme.mark_scheme:
Correct entities connected (Members–Loans, Loans–Books) (1)
Members 1 — M Loans (1)
Loans M — 1 Books (1)
scheme.model_answer: Members 1 —— M Loans M —— 1 Books

parts.title: Foreign keys
parts.text: Identify the field(s) that can be used as foreign keys in `Loans`, and state what each one links to.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberID — links to Members (1)
BookID — links to Books (1)
Do not award a mark if only one field is given without the other.
scheme.model_answer: MemberID links each loan to a member; BookID links each loan to a book.

parts.title: Members and Books
parts.text: Explain the relationship between `Members` and `Books`, and why the `Loans` table is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Members and Books have a many-to-many relationship: a member borrows many books; a book is borrowed by many members (over time) (1)
- an M:M relationship cannot be created directly (1)
- Loans is the link table that turns it into two one-to-many relationships (and stores LoanDate etc.) (1)
scheme.model_answer: A member can borrow many books and a book can be borrowed by many members, so the relationship is many-to-many. This cannot be stored directly, so Loans acts as a link table, giving Members 1—M Loans and Books 1—M Loans, and also stores the loan dates.

questions.title: A football league
questions.text:
A football league stores data about **teams**, **players**, **stadiums** and **sponsors**.

- Each team plays its home games in one stadium; each stadium belongs to one team.
- A team has many players; each player plays for one team.
- A team can have many sponsors, and a sponsor can sponsor many teams.

parts.title: Relationship types
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Team–Stadium 1:1 (1); Team–Player 1:M (1); Team–Sponsor M:M (1)

parts.title: Implement Team–Player
parts.text: Explain how the relationship between Team and Player is created in the database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- TeamID, the primary key of Teams (1)
- is added as a foreign key to the Players table (the many side) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The primary key TeamID of the Teams table is stored as a foreign key in the Players table.

parts.title: Implement Team–Sponsor
parts.text: Explain how the relationship between Team and Sponsor is implemented. Name the fields of any new table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A link table, e.g. Sponsorships (1)
- with fields TeamID and SponsorID (foreign keys / composite primary key) (1)
scheme.model_answer: A link table Sponsorships(TeamID, SponsorID) is created, whose two foreign keys form a composite primary key.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the ERD for the league, including the link entity from part (c).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Teams 1 — 1 Stadiums and Teams 1 — M Players (1)
Link entity added between Teams and Sponsors (1)
Teams 1 — M link and Sponsors 1 — M link (1)
scheme.model_answer: Stadiums 1 — 1 Teams 1 — M Players; Teams 1 — M Sponsorships M — 1 Sponsors

questions.title: An online shop
questions.text:
An online shop is designing its database.

```text
Customers  ( CustomerID, Name, Email )
Orders     ( OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate )
Products   ( ProductID, Name, Price )
OrderLines ( OrderID, ProductID, Quantity )
```

parts.title: Customers and Orders
parts.text: State the type of relationship between `Customers` and `Orders` and justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme: One-to-many (1); one customer can place many orders but each order belongs to one customer / CustomerID is a foreign key in Orders (1)
scheme.model_answer: One-to-many: a customer can place many orders, but each order is placed by one customer, so CustomerID appears in Orders as a foreign key.

parts.title: Purpose of OrderLines
parts.text: Explain why the `OrderLines` table is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Orders and Products have a many-to-many relationship (an order contains many products; a product is in many orders) (1)
- OrderLines is the link table that resolves it into two 1:M relationships (and stores the quantity) (1)
scheme.model_answer: An order can contain many products and a product can be in many orders, a many-to-many relationship; OrderLines is the link table that turns it into two one-to-many relationships and stores the quantity of each product.

parts.title: Keys of OrderLines
parts.text: Tick (✓) the boxes to show the role of each field in `OrderLines`. A field may have more than one tick.

scheme.mark_scheme: OrderID: PK ✓ FK ✓ (1); ProductID: PK ✓ FK ✓ (1); Quantity: neither (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: One mark per fully correct row.

parts.title: Draw the ERD
parts.text: Draw the entity-relationship diagram for the shop's database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Customers 1 — M Orders (1)
Orders 1 — M OrderLines (1)
Products 1 — M OrderLines (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customers 1 —— M Orders 1 —— M OrderLines M —— 1 Products

questions.title: A school sports centre
questions.text:
A school sports centre stores data about **coaches**, **teams**, **pupils** and **lockers**.

- Each team has one coach; a coach can train several teams.
- A team has many pupils, and a pupil can play in several teams.
- Each coach has one locker, and each locker belongs to one coach.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Any one of Coach / Team / Pupil / Locker (1)
- A second, different entity (1)

points.criterion: Any one of Coach / Team / Pupil / Locker

scheme.model_answer: Coach and Team.

parts.title: Attributes
parts.text: State **two** attributes that could be stored for the entity **Pupil**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- One suitable attribute, e.g. PupilID / name / class / date of birth (1)
- A second suitable attribute (1)

points.criterion: One suitable attribute, e.g. PupilID / name / class / date of birth

scheme.model_answer: PupilID and Name.

parts.title: Relationship types
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of relationship.

scheme.mark_scheme: Coach–Team 1:M (1); Team–Pupil M:M (1); Coach–Locker 1:1 (1)

parts.title: Relationship
parts.text: Define the term **relationship** in a database.

scheme.mark_scheme: - A link / association between two entities (tables) (1)

points.criterion: A link / association between two entities (tables)

scheme.model_answer: A link between two entities, showing how their records are connected.

summary: Entities, attributes and relationships; one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships; how relationships are created with primary and foreign keys and link tables; and how to read and draw entity-relationship diagrams (ERDs).

blocks.content: A **thing (person, object, place or event)** about which data is stored — for example *Student*, *Book*, *Order*. Each entity becomes a **table** in a relational database.
A **property** of an entity — one item of data stored about it, e.g. *StudentID*, *Name*, *DateOfBirth*. Each attribute becomes a **field (column)**.

A **link between two entities** that shows how their records are connected, e.g. *a teacher **teaches** many classes*. In a database a relationship is created with a **primary key** in one table and a matching **foreign key** in another.

A diagram that shows the **entities** in a system (as boxes), the **relationships** between them (as lines), and the **degree (cardinality)** of each relationship — one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. It is drawn during the **design** stage, before the tables are created.

blocks.title: The three types of relationship
rows: Each record in A is linked to **at most one** record in B, and each record in B to **one** in A
Country — Capital city; Person — Passport; Student — Locker
One record in A is linked to **many** records in B, but each record in B is linked to **only one** in A
Publisher — Titles; Class — Pupils; Customer — Orders
One record in A is linked to **many** in B **and** one record in B is linked to **many** in A
Students — Courses; Actors — Films; Products — Orders

blocks.content:
Ask the question **in both directions**:
1. "Can one **Publisher** have many **Titles**?" — **Yes**.
2. "Can one **Title** have many **Publishers**?" — **No**.
One "yes" and one "no" → **one-to-many** (the "many" is on the Titles side). Two "yes" → many-to-many. Two "no" → one-to-one.

blocks.caption: ERD notation — crow's foot and labels
One-to-many: one publisher publishes many titles

blocks.title: How each relationship is implemented
columns: How it is created in the database
rows: The **primary key** of the "one" table is placed as a **foreign key** in the "many" table. *`pub_ID` (PK of Publishers) is a foreign key in Titles.*
The primary key of one table is a foreign key in the other (which must be **unique**), or the two tables are combined into one.
**Cannot be created directly.** It is replaced by a **link (junction) table** whose primary key is usually a **composite key** of the two foreign keys, giving **two 1:M** relationships.

blocks.title: Resolving a many-to-many relationship
blocks.content:
*A student takes many courses; a course has many students.*

```text
Students    ( _StudentID_, Name, Grade )
Courses     ( _CourseID_, CourseName, Room )
Enrolments  ( _StudentID*_, _CourseID*_, StartDate )      <- link table, composite key
```
`Students 1 —— M Enrolments M —— 1 Courses`

blocks.caption: The link table turns M:M into two 1:M relationships

items.title: Why M:M must be resolved
items.content:
- A field can hold **only one value** (atomic), so a student record cannot list all its courses in one field.
- The link table stores **one record per pairing** (student + course) and can hold extra data about the pairing (start date, mark).

items.title: Reading the foreign key
items.content:
- The table that **contains the foreign key** is on the **"many"** side of a 1:M relationship.
- *`course_tbl` contains `StudentID` → one student has many course records → `student_tbl` 1 — M `course_tbl`.*

blocks.title: Describing a relationship (exam style)
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe the type of relationship between tables `student_tbl` and `course_tbl`.**
`student_tbl` (primary key `StudentID`) links to the **foreign key** `StudentID` in `course_tbl` (1); the relationship is **one-to-many** — one student can appear in many course records (1).

blocks.title: How to draw an ERD from a description
items: **Find the entities** — the nouns about which data is stored (each becomes a table).
**List the attributes** of each entity and choose a **primary key**.
**Find the relationships** — the verbs that link entities (*places*, *teaches*, *borrows*).
**Decide the degree** of each relationship by asking the question in both directions.
**Resolve every M:M** relationship with a link table.
**Draw** the boxes and lines, marking each end **1** or **M** (or a crow's foot); add the **foreign keys** on the "many" side.

blocks.title: Worked example — a product supply system
blocks.content:
*Stores order products. Each delivery is made to one store and contains one product; a store receives many deliveries and a product appears in many deliveries.*

```text
Stores     ( _Store_code_, Name, City )
Products   ( _Product_code_, Name, Price )
Deliveries ( _Delivery_ID_, Store_code*, Product_code*, Date, Quantity )
```
Relationships: **Stores 1 — M Deliveries** and **Products 1 — M Deliveries**. (Deliveries is the link that resolves the M:M relationship between stores and products.)

blocks.caption: ERD for the product supply system

blocks.title: Worked example — a school
blocks.content:
*A teacher can be the form tutor of one class only, and each class has one form tutor. A class has many pupils; each pupil belongs to one class. Pupils take many clubs; each club has many pupils.*

| Relationship | Degree | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Teacher — Class (form tutor) | **1:1** | `TutorID` (unique) in Classes |
| Class — Pupil | **1:M** | `ClassID` foreign key in Pupils |
| Pupil — Club | **M:M** | Link table `Memberships(PupilID, ClubID)` |

blocks.title: Drawing ERDs on the platform
blocks.content: In the diagram questions, add an **entity** for each table (name on the first line, attributes below), connect two entities with a line, then **select the line** to set its cardinality: **1:1**, **1:M**, **M:1** or **M:M**.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Build the ER diagram for the given Books database (Publishers, Titles). [2]**
Two entities **Publishers** and **Titles** (1) joined by a **one-to-many** relationship, with the "many" at Titles (1).

**Q: Explain the type of connection between the entities. [1]**
One item from the **Publishers** table may have **many** related items in the **Titles** table (one-to-many).

**Q: Draw the E–R diagram for `student_tbl`, `course_tbl` and `courseteacher_tbl`. [2]**
`student_tbl` **1 — M** `course_tbl` (1); `course_tbl` **M — 1** `courseteacher_tbl` (1).

- Putting the "many" (crow's foot) at the wrong end — it goes at the table that holds the **foreign key**.
- Leaving a **many-to-many** relationship without a link table in the database design.
- Drawing **attributes as separate entities**.
- Writing "one-to-many" without saying **which** side is "many".
- Forgetting to check the relationship **in both directions**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define entity, attribute, relationship and ERD.
Give a real example of a 1:1, a 1:M and an M:M relationship.
Where is the foreign key placed in a one-to-many relationship?
How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
Draw the ERD for: *a customer places many orders; an order contains many products*.
